25578a6e43c5: What did Bill W. say about clubs and A.A.?
e006f4a59e70: Bill W. was for clubs, for the members who want them. In 1947 he wrote that A.A.s who need and want clubs ought to have them, and that the real question was how to keep their troubles smaller than their benefits.
077f0a47ed93: But a club is not A.A. Experience in New York taught that a club should be separately incorporated under another name, run and paid for by the people who want it, and kept out of the A.A. groups' hands.
98d5889fbbee: The Long Form of Tradition Six says the same: clubs are "secondary aids" that should be set apart so the groups can drop them if they need to, and they shouldn't use the A.A. name.
712cdcc9d136: Bill warned against treating club life as a substitute for the program, a "Thirteenth Step."
932d6adb71bb: <0>Clubs were popular, and so was the opposition.</0> Bill opens by saying clubs had become part of A.A. life, and that a vote would bring a large "yes" (P-17, p. 17). He then names the danger on that side: some members acted as if a club were a sort of "Thirteenth Step" without which the other Steps wouldn't work, and they "are apt to depend upon clubs rather than upon the A.A. program" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947, p. 17). A strong minority wanted no clubs at all, pointing to clubs that turned into hangouts, fights over money and authority, and bad publicity (P-17, p. 17).
ac51ab8659ae: <0>His middle ground.</0> "A.A.s who need and want clubs ought to have them" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947, p. 18). The question was how to make them assets and keep their liabilities down (P-17, p. 18).
eeb9dcbd7fb0: <0>What New York learned the hard way.</0> Bill tells the story of the first club, at West 24th Street, as an average example, not a model (P-17, p. 18). Meetings had outgrown homes, a restaurant lacked the home atmosphere, and the members took over a former artists' club (P-17, p. 18). Then came the growing pains: dictators, drunks disrupting meetings, rent trouble, and a corporation whose directors seemed to compete with the A.A. rotating committee (P-17, pp. 18–19). The lease-holding corporation was named "Alcoholics Anonymous of New York, Inc.," and Bill admits they had effectively incorporated the whole state (P-17, p. 19). When the suburban groups grew, Manhattan expected them to pay for the club and its secretary; they never did, and the club, the area's common needs and the A.A. work stayed knotted together for a long time (P-17, pp. 19–20).
d6042ece8cdd: <0>The lesson.</0> The tangle came apart when they saw that clubs "ought to be strictly the business of those individuals who specially want clubs, and who are willing to pay for them" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947, p. 20). A club should be separately incorporated under another name; its directors should look after club business only; and an A.A. group should never get into running a business (P-17, p. 20). If the A.A. committee tries to boss the club, or the club tries to run the groups, there is trouble at once; the only cure found was "to separate the material from the spiritual" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947, p. 20). A group meeting in a club pays rent or splits the collection (P-17, p. 20).
f3072dd97acb: <0>Who belongs, who pays.</0> Bill says plainly they didn't yet know all the answers (P-17, p. 21). His suggestion: any A.A. member should be free to enjoy a club whether he contributes or not, and regular contributors should vote for the club's directors (P-17, p. 21). Large gifts to buy or build clubs lead to headaches, and public solicitation is "extremely dangerous" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947, p. 21).
8ff23d7d8518: <0>Where clubs end up.</0> Outside small towns, A.A. outgrows any clubhouse, and the shared work of an area (hospital arrangements, a central office, local public relations) passes to a central or intergroup committee that every A.A. has an interest in, club member or not (P-17, pp. 21–22). The club is left outside, "where, in the opinion of many, it should be" (P-17, "Clubs in A.A.", 1947, p. 22).
668bdee77341: The Long Form of Tradition Six (1946)
6e7692d83b9d: The Long Form puts the same experience into one paragraph. Any considerable property of real use to A.A. should be separately incorporated and managed, "thus dividing the material from the spiritual" (p. 564). An A.A. group shouldn't go into business. Secondary aids "such as clubs or hospitals" should be incorporated and set apart so that, if necessary, "they can be freely discarded by the groups" (p. 564). They shouldn't use the A.A. name, and they should be managed by those who pay for them. "For clubs, A.A. managers are usually preferred" (p. 564), while hospitals belong well outside A.A.
6702c8db12c8: A year earlier Bill had already said club support should be an individual matter, not a group matter (P-17, p. 29). Groups in an area could fairly pay for a central-office secretary who serves them all, but it isn't a group or central-committee job to fund clubs, and "the majority ought not to try to coerce" the minority into paying for clubs they don't want (P-17, "Money", 1946, p. 29).
c6a1d32e1d6e: The 2018 pamphlet <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16) carries this forward: owning and managing real estate isn't a group function, so "technically, there is no such thing as an" A.A. club (P-16, 2018, p. 40). Clubs are run by members acting as private individuals through separate nonprofit corporations, and the General Service Office doesn't take contributions from clubs (P-16, pp. 40–41).

0660ec81a82d: Bill grounds it in Tradition Two, first printed in 1946: one ultimate authority, "a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience" (p. 563).
a6683c078529: Concept I is about world services. It doesn't give anyone authority over a group's own affairs.
8b1782f057cd: The earlier text first: Tradition Two (1946)
644239f0d5cc: The Long Form of Tradition Two: "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience" (p. 563). Long Form Nine adds that the trustees are, "in effect, our A.A. General Service Committee" (p. 565), and that A.A.'s servants "derive no real authority from their titles; they do not govern" (p. 565).
5ff14432c855: In 1947 Bill described the trustees of the Alcoholic Foundation as "simple custodians" of the office, the Grapevine, A.A.'s funds and Traditions: "caretakers only" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947).
f6ae800f80a5: So in 1946–47 the principle was already stated. What hadn't been settled was how the groups, scattered across the world, could actually hold authority over the New York office and its board. Concept I tells how that was done.
6a2c7b886821: What Bill's Concept I essay says (1962)
0f32f4807908: <0>The claim.</0> "The A.A. groups today hold ultimate responsibility and final authority for our world services" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). World services are the things no single group or area can do: uniform literature, public relations, answering pleas for help, helping new groups form, a magazine, translations.
b655dd787b57: <0>The history.</0> In 1938 Bill and Dr. Bob, with nonalcoholic friends, formed a trusteeship, the Alcoholic Foundation, renamed the General Service Board in 1954. By 1950 membership had grown from about 50 to 100,000 and the Traditions had been written and adopted. Yet few members knew the trustees existed: "Not one member in a thousand could tell who our Trustees were" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). The trustees controlled money, but on policy they turned to the two founders.
0f12bb7694ca: <0>The turning point.</0> In 1948 it became known that Dr. Bob was fatally ill. "The fact had to be faced that A.A.’s founders were perishable" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). Many trustees and members opposed calling a representative conference, fearing politics, expense and strife; Bill says those arguments "were not without merit." But "For the first time it was seen that only a representative conference could take the place of Dr. Bob and me" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). The first Conference met experimentally in 1951; "The groups assumed that responsibility at the St. Louis International Convention of 1955" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I), where Bill made the transfer on behalf of Dr. Bob, the trustees and the old-timers.
d4e65c669f1e: <0>The reason in principle.</0> Bill quotes Tradition Two in full and says its principles are "crystal clear: the A.A. groups are to be the final authority; their leaders are to be entrusted with delegated responsibilities only" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). He notes "Tradition Two had been written in 1945" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I), but it took until 1955 for everyone to be convinced it applied to the trustees and founders as well: "It took five years more for all of us to be convinced that Tradition Two was for everybody" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I).
3b01069cd246: <0>Group conscience.</0> Bill admits the phrase is vague to many members, and contrasts A.A. with democracies where ignorance, apathy and power-seeking erode self-government. A.A.'s safeguard, he says, is that each life and group is built on the Steps and Traditions, and "the penalty for extensive disobedience to these principles is death for the individual and dissolution for the group" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I), together with the love members have for one another.
b4e952090905: <0>Not God's job alone.</0> One detail cuts against an easy faith: in the boom years of 1945–50, many members thought nothing could happen to A.A. "because God was protecting A.A." (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). Bill calls that attitude a strange contrast with how carefully members guarded their own sobriety, and says planning ahead was needed.
a3c5788becb9: How the authority is actually used
1533026f1e3b: Concept I gives the groups ultimate authority, and the next Concepts explain why they don't use it directly: they delegate the active work to the Conference (Concept II), give servants a Right of Decision (Concept III), and so on. See <0>Who has the final say in A.A.?</0> for how the pieces fit.

bd3148e6a498: <0>Why charters aren't enough.</0> The Conference Charter is broad and "can be variously construed." 91ff9057edc0: <0>Three possible answers.</0> Throw away all charters and job descriptions (anarchy); add rules for every contingency ("altogether too much red tape"); or trust leaders, within their framework, to decide how to apply their authority to each situation as it comes up. 9f0a466a6543: <0>No superiors at the ballot.</0> On the board's committees too, trustees, outside experts and staff sit together and vote. "When the time comes to ballot, there are no ‘superiors,’ no ‘inferiors,’ and no ‘advisers’" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IV).
dec28b0c4591: <0>The one exception.</0> "Members holding paid staff positions cannot become Trustees" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IV). It would interfere with the trustees' four-year rotation, and paid trustees could become a vested interest the Conference couldn't dislodge if the board ever had to be reorganized. Staff are still invited to the board's quarterly meetings, where they can speak but not vote.
e64f17b8716f: <0>How it was learned.</0> In the early years the trustees held all the authority and the money, while Bill, his assistant and her staff did the work with "practically no authority." Two trustee committees issued orders, sometimes conflicting ones; Bill's assistant, who carried most of the office load, couldn't get into a trustees' meeting. Then the publishing company's treasurer, an old friend of Bill's, tore up the staff's paychecks because they'd been issued two days early so the office workers could buy Easter bonnets. "Right then and there we began to wonder how much absolute authority over money and people any one of us drunks could handle" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IV). Bill's conclusion is that no one objects to final authority as such: "We are only against its misapplication or misuse" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IV).
2ad52d013d46: <0>Arguments he expected, and his answers.</0> - <1>Delegates will try to take away the trustees' and staff's Conference vote.</1> Bill agrees they should refrain from voting on reports of their own past performance, but says most Conference business is about the future, and their knowledge is needed. A footnote adds that delegates meet only a few days a year and can't know every problem firsthand. - <2>Trustees and staff might swing a close vote.</2> "But why not?" He notes they had never voted as a bloc. - <3>Groups might send delegates irrevocably instructed.</3> Then the delegates "would feel like agents and order-takers" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IV), not participants.

"Just as there are no second-class AA’s, neither should there be any second-class world service workers, either" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IV). bcc1db213370: <0>Why minorities.</0> Minorities "frequently can be right" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V), and even when wrong they force a thorough debate. "The well-heard minority, therefore, is our chief protection against an uninformed, misinformed, hasty or angry majority" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).
78107e644507: <0>Petition.</0> Bill expected it to be seldom used, but "its very existence will always tend to restrain those in authority from unjust uses of their power" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). Workers should accept the direction their jobs need, but needn't "silently endure unnecessary and unfair personal domination."
b26c0c16f820: <0>A.A.'s charter of liberties.</0> "In Alcoholics Anonymous individual freedom is of enormous importance" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). A member belongs the moment he says so, and "Neither can we force our members to believe anything or pay anything" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).
e9e0409d0658: <0>Trusting a qualified minority.</0> The group conscience can't act directly in most world service matters because it can't be fully informed, and in a time of great disturbance it may not act wisely. So A.A. trusts "a small but truly qualified minority" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V), the hundred-odd members of the Conference, to act for it, keeping the power to recall and replace them.
24cfe9b23610: <0>Examples in 1962.</0> - Electing delegates: without two-thirds, the majority's candidate goes into a hat with the minority's choices, and lots are drawn. 8eb94762aa37: <0>De Tocqueville.</0> Bill closes with the French writer's warning against the "tyranny" of apathetic, self-seeking, uninformed or angry majorities, and adds the other danger: "the even worse tyranny of very small minorities invested with absolute power" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). A.A., he says, needs no government that enforces conformity by punishment, only a service structure that holds up the Traditions and carries the message.

Once a sound structure exists, that job is mostly done; leadership has to be found again and again.

6961d4e4bd2e: <0>Choosing by lot.</0> Some members doubted the Third Legacy method (two-thirds or the hat). 5b40674ac78f: <0>The main theme: the trustees replacing the founders.</0> Bill says he is still advising and finishing leftover chores from 1955, these Concepts among them, but will soon have to withdraw from nearly all world service work. The board ran from 1938 to 1951 without a Conference; that change was resisted but proved right. Now he believes the board's leadership strength must be "considerably increased." "Students of history recognize that the transference of the original leadership of a society to its successors in leadership is always a critical turning point" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX).
b90f73e5cea5: <0>The 1959 article, "Leadership in A.A.: Ever a Vital Need."</0> Bill offers it for future servants. Its points: - A.A. sometimes twists "principles before personalities" so far that leaders become faceless automatons; at other times it demands they be practically infallible. Real leaders are in between. - "In effect, we are saying to them," Bill writes, "Act for us, but don’t boss us" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). - If a leader power-drives, members rebel; if he only takes orders, "he really isn’t a leader at all." - Good leadership originates plans, but consults widely on new and important matters, and "will often discard its own cherished plans for others that are better, and it will give credit to the source" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). - "Good leadership never passes the buck" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). - A statesman, unlike a "politico," knows that even large majorities can sometimes be dead wrong, and will stand against them when something vital is at stake. But opposition for its own sake is fatal: "When called upon, leadership must always give its reasons, and good ones" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). - Give and take: progress comes through "a series of improving compromises," yet sometimes one must "stick flat-footed" to a conviction. - Criticism: listen carefully to constructive critics, and even to destructive ones, because they may be telling the whole truth or a little of it. - Vision: the ability to make good estimates of the future. Bill says "One day at a time" refers to our emotional lives, not to refusing to plan. "As a matter of fact, all of A.A.’s Twelve Traditions were at first questions of estimate and vision for the future" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX), and he gives self-support and anonymity as examples. - Talents differ; choosing the best talent isn't creating a privileged class.
4d7fcfc7644e: <0>Twelfth Step work.</0> Bill ends by applying this to the work nearly every member does: "Every sponsor is necessarily a leader" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept IX). The sponsor in his example is working with "his prospects," a person's life and family in the balance, and must estimate reactions, time his approach and lead "by personal spiritual example." This is the same situation as Chapter 7 of the Big Book, going to a man who is still drinking, though the Big Book's first 164 pages don't use the word sponsor (it appears only in the personal stories).

26c91e81fa14: Bill W.'s reason, written in 1962: if people are given a job without the authority to do it, or authority without a defined limit, "personal clashes, confusion, and ineffectiveness will be inevitable" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X).
0e85de5286ba: Final authority must sit somewhere at each level, but should "practically never be used in full, except in an emergency" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X). 0584e0fd2749: Bill calls it all implied in Tradition Two: the group conscience as the ultimate authority, the trusted servant as the delegated one. "One cannot function without the other" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X).

fab4f06b8123: <0>The principle.</0> Most societies and governments of the day, Bill says, break the rule that each responsibility needs a matching authority. The earlier Concepts were written to define the authority and responsibility of the groups, the Conference, the trustees and the service corporations so that they match at every level.
d404e79df252: <0>Four conditions.</0> Things go wrong unless authority and responsibility are well defined; those with final authority are able and willing to delegate; those with delegated authority feel free to use it as trusted servants; and there is some definite way to settle doubtful cases.
d27d53eaf35d: <0>A line of final authority.</0> "The principle of ultimate authority runs clear through our structure" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X): groups over the Conference, delegates over the trustees, trustees over the service corporations, directors over officers, officers over staff. Everything has to "head up somewhere" so each worker knows who the final boss is.
a07a3d332bca: <0>But not used in full.</0> Without delegated authority, Bill pictures groups directing delegates on every vote, delegates turning trustees into "a timid committee," trustees running the corporations by directive, and executives becoming "small czars." The proper uses of final authority are emergencies: groups can elect better delegates or withhold funds; delegates can censure or reorganize the trustees; trustees can do the same with the corporations; corporations can fire executives.
43d7fd49d244: <0>How authority is defined.</0> By legal means (corporate charters), by traditional means, and by principles for settling doubtful cases. The Conference Charter "is not a legal instrument, but practically speaking it is the substance of a contract between the A.A. groups and their Conference" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X). Delegates vote their conscience and the Conference decides what to refer back to the groups; the trustees insist on their legal right to administer, with a veto in rare cases; the corporations' charters and non-trustee directors protect their operating authority.
20167e7b87f2: <0>Conflicts.</0> Interlocking memberships between committees and corporations settle most routine conflicts. For the rest, there must be a senior jurisdiction, the junior one must be heard, and there must always be a known point of final decision.
888779ad9bc4: <0>No double-headed management.</0> "A condition to be avoided at all costs is double-headed business or policy management" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X). Bill takes this up again under Concept XI.
8557668f05c2: <0>Two more safeguards.</0> The Rights of Appeal and Petition, because "a bare majority is apt to constitute itself as a pseudo-ultimate authority" and executives "are apt to over-boss their assistants."
3570a92e2de6: <0>Summed up.</0> Be sure there is plenty of final authority to correct or reorganize, and equally sure every trusted servant has a clearly defined and adequate authority to do the daily work.
47184aacef01: The General Policy Committee Bill describes is now the General Sharing Session, meeting three times a year for about two hours; its functions "have changed markedly" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept X, footnote 1).

9d21b67ca462: <0>Why these people matter.</0> The non-trustee committee members, directors, executives and staff do most of the work, travel, meet visitors, and are what members see of world service. "Their quality and dedication, or their lack of these characteristics, will make or break our structure of service" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). They don't just support the trustees' leadership; they share it.
0194f34554ed: <0>The committees (as of 1962).</0> - <1>Nominating</1> fills vacancies with the best people available. Bill warns of a quiet decline: "Instinctively we look for associates rather like ourselves, only a little less experienced and able" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). - <2>Finance and Budgetary</2> keeps A.A. solvent. "This is the place where money and spirituality do have to mix, and in just the right proportion" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). Bill also tells how an earlier drive to build the reserve let the office run down, and group contributions fell by tens of thousands a year: prudence isn't hoarding. - <3>Public Information</3> needs professionals who can adapt to "Attraction rather than promotion"; "the techniques used to sell a big time personality or a new hair lotion would not be for A.A." (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). One public blunder could turn new prospects away. - <4>Literature</4> revises and creates books and pamphlets. Bill says the policy is "to aim at only the best," that a key figure "will necessarily be a paid writer and consultant" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI), and that getting the "A.A. feel" into the writing is vital. - <5>General Policy</5> filters business for the board, with minority reports, in long Sunday sessions.
64b6172ed9df: None of these committees is executive; they recommend.
3e1fa4a8ccfa: <0>The two corporations.</0> A.A. World Services (with its publishing division) and the Grapevine each have their own board of directors, made up of trustees, outside experts and paid executives. Bill explains why they shouldn't be merged with each other or with the board, and why publishing needn't be a separate company: "Most of our A.A. books are already written, and it is probable that not many more will be published" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI).
967b5374eafe: <0>Four principles for paid workers.</0> 1. <1>One executive.</1> "A board or a committee can never actively manage anything, in the continuous executive sense" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). Executive direction heads up in one person, who should be left alone while the work is done well, and who must learn when to act alone and when to consult. 2. <2>Fair pay.</2> Each paid worker "should be recompensed in reasonable relation to the value of his or her similar services or abilities in the commercial world" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). Bill rejects the idea that A.A. workers should accept charity-level pay, which would ask of them a sacrifice asked of no other member. Cheap help, he says, is insecure and costly: "This is neither good spirituality nor good business" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). 3. <3>Rotation.</3> Staff rotate assignments and are paid on the same basis, after an early collapse showed the danger of one highly paid person holding everything. On terms of service: "a Delegate has to serve two years, and a Trustee must serve four" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI), but staff shouldn't have a fixed term. 4. <4>Full participation.</4> Paid workers get votes on boards and committees, and more: they should be treated as friends and co-workers, and the fact that they depend on their pay should never be used as a lever against them.
d8fb7e104738: <0>A line to read in its context.</0> Explaining why members shouldn't see world service as charity they pay for, Bill writes that the services benefit members as much as newcomers: "We are helping others in order to help ourselves" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XI). That is his 1962 wording about service funding. Chapter 7 of the Big Book (1939) is the earlier text on why we help others: it too says plainly that helping others protects the helper's sobriety (pp. 89, 97), and it keeps turning the helper toward the other man's welfare (p. 94) (see <1>Is helping others selfish if it keeps me sober?</1>).
1d02a49f2bb4: Six more trustees' committees have been added since 1962 (footnote 1); the General Policy Committee became the General Sharing Session (footnote 2).
d6a7d0fbd0ae: GSO has had a full-time general manager since 1960; the Grapevine now has a full-time paid editorial staff; most GSO staff now rotate every two years (footnotes 6–8).

c8f3cafd3e35: Concept XII: what are the General Warranties of the Conference?
248f3c761b1e: Concept XII is Article 12 of the Conference Charter (1955): six promises binding the General Service Conference to "observe the spirit of the A.A. Tradition" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). In order: never the seat of perilous wealth or power; enough operating funds plus an ample reserve; no member in unqualified authority over another; important decisions by discussion, vote and, whenever possible, substantial unanimity; no punitive action and no public controversy; never any acts of government, and always democratic.
0dbba7352a18: It is the hardest Concept to change. The Conference can amend the rest of its Charter, but changing a Warranty needs the written consent of three-quarters of the groups that respond, with six months to consider.
79f1d5d2e26e: Bill W.'s 1962 essay calls them "counsels of prudence" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII), protection against "our very natural human temptations to wealth, prestige, power, and the like."
8f51e4a183a1: Several of the Warranties echo what the 1946 Long Form already said to the groups: prudent reserves, no large gifts, no controversy, "they do not govern" (p. 565).
e2f9cfadfc47: <0>Wealth and reserves.</0> Long Form Seven (1946): accepting large gifts or gifts with obligations "is unwise," and "we view with much concern those A.A. treasuries which continue, beyond prudent reserves, to accumulate funds for no stated A.A. purpose" (p. 564).
f16a6c3204c8: <0>Authority.</0> Long Form Nine: A.A.'s servants "do not govern" (p. 565). Bill in 1947: "So long as we avoid any menacing accumulation of wealth or the growth of personal government at these centers, we cannot go astray" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947).
a33c8e78041c: <0>Controversy.</0> Long Form Ten: "The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one" (p. 565).
8acfa1fc9ba1: <0>Freedom.</0> Long Form Three: membership never to depend "upon money or conformity" (p. 563).
e93b980c868a: Concept XII turns these into promises made by the Conference itself.
b7786fed26c8: The Warranties and how they're protected
6342407bb4a5: The Concept "consists of Article 12 of the Conference Charter" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII), the 1955 agreement between the groups and their trustees. The first eleven Articles "can be readily amended by the Conference itself." Article 12 needs the written consent of three-quarters of the directory-listed groups who vote, with six months to deliberate. "Although changes in the Warranties of Article 12 thus have been made difficult, they have not been made impossible" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). Bill ranks them with the Traditions for world service.
b890af4ae8db: What Bill's essay says about each (1962)
3b0a2db6dd35: <0>One: never the seat of perilous wealth or power.</0> Not "no money, no authority," which would be "dangerous and absurd." The protection against wealth is the Tradition itself: decline outside contributions and keep individual gifts modest, and "we need only to avoid the temptation of taking money from the outside world" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). On a would-be dictator: "Our setup being what it is, such an aspirant couldn’t last a year" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII), since the delegates control the money. The one power the Conference can't do without is the spiritual kind, from humble and dedicated servants: "They do not drive us by mandate; they lead us by example" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).
f500d084f4b5: <0>Two: sufficient funds plus an ample reserve.</0> Members give time freely but are slower with money. The reserve then was about one year's office expenses, saved over twenty years mostly from book income, and it had covered the years when contributions fell short. Bill answers critics who wanted the Big Book sold at cost: charity to newcomers is the sponsor's, not the group's or A.A.'s: "But such charities are the responsibility of the sponsor and not of the A.A. group itself" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). Book income, he argues, isn't really profit but the sum of buyers' contributions: "This fund is not the property of private investors; it is wholly owned by A.A. itself" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). He also addresses his own royalties: "This royalty income from the book buyers has enabled me to do all the rest of my A.A. work on a full-time volunteer basis" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII), and hopes the arrangement will continue to be considered fair.
7c4e466dd0db: <0>Three: no unqualified authority.</0> This makes the Right of Participation (Concept IV) something the Conference alone can't take away. More broadly, "It really means that we of A.A. will not tolerate absolute human authority in any form" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). Some members already called Article 12 "The A.A. Service Bill of Rights."
e6ca9a53019d: <0>Four: substantial unanimity.</0> Debate should continue, time permitting, until a heavy majority can support each critical decision; then even a bad decision brings no recriminations. But there are limits: in an emergency, or when "a small minority obstinately tries to use the principle of substantial unanimity to block a clearly needed action," then "it would be the plain duty of the majority to override such a misuse of the principle of substantial unanimity" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).
ba18c21c827f: <0>Five: no punishment, no public controversy.</0> "When we of A.A. fail to follow sound spiritual principles, alcohol cuts us down" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII), so no human system of penalties is needed. Under public attack that has little or no justification, the best defense is almost always none, "complete silence at the public level"; justified criticism may be acknowledged privately, with thanks. On Tradition violators: the Conference is "guardian" of the Traditions, but suing or publicly punishing them "would place the Conference in the position of having violated one A.A. Tradition in order to defend another" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). Privately it can tell them they're out of order and use persuasion; in the long run it relies on A.A. and public opinion. Bill notes that "A.A.’s World Headquarters is not a police operation" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII), and that many local Tradition questions are gray areas best left to the people concerned.
b4c825688cec: On a split in A.A., Bill's answer is near-complete nonresistance: "We have no doctrine that has to be maintained" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). Members who want their own groups, retreats or Communion breakfasts are welcome to them: "Only we hope you won’t designate your efforts as an A.A. group or enterprise" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). A.A. will give away its knowledge and experience, "all excepting the A.A. name itself" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).
d86b7b3dfa41: On protecting the name: A.A. once considered incorporating it everywhere and asking Congress for a charter, but the early Conferences decided against it, since a public lawsuit is a public controversy. Bill refers readers to <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957) for the story, which prints the committee's finding that a Congressional incorporation "would create by law a power to govern" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957) contrary to the Traditions.
ca2c976e33ed: <0>Six: no acts of government; always democratic.</0> Bill lists the freedoms the Traditions give: no penalties for nonconformity, no fees or dues, no expulsion, each group running its own affairs, and any group of alcoholics gathered for sobriety may call itself an A.A. group "provided that, as a group, they have no other purpose or affiliation" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII). The Conference must "abstain completely from any and all acts of authoritative government which could in any wise curtail A.A.’s freedom under God" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).
85e7097a6b77: <0>"No other purpose or affiliation."</0> Long Form Three (1946) says a group may call itself an A.A. group "provided that, as a group, they have no other affiliation" (p. 563). Bill's 1962 list adds "purpose."
77b9addb0251: <0>The original wording.</0> The 1955 Charter's Article 12 read "an incitement to serious public controversy" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955). The current Charter and the Concept say "public controversy," without "serious." Our copy doesn't say when it changed.
48d4a10a35a2: <0>Two-thirds, then three-quarters.</0> The 1955 Charter as first printed required the written consent of two-thirds of all groups to change the Tradition; the St. Louis resolution the same year asked for three-quarters of the registered groups who respond. The 1957 Conference amended the Charter to three-quarters, covering Article 12, the Traditions and the Steps (Appendix K, footnote 4); a 1976 resolution confirmed the Steps (Appendix L, footnote 3).
56c1183c0b16: <0>The name.</0> Bill's 1962 text says the Conference decided against legal protection of the name. A 2024–2026 footnote adds: "However, the name Alcoholics Anonymous and the abbreviation A.A. were all legally registered in 1972" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII, footnote 3).
800be3b08539: <0>The reserve.</0> Bill's 1960 reserve was about one year's office expenses. P-8 (© 2017) says the reserve "should be one full year’s operating expenses" (P-8). The 2024–2026 footnote reports 6.47 months at the end of 2024.

The Concepts were written by Bill W. in 1962 and describe how A.A.'s world service bodies (the General Service Conference, the trustees, the service corporations and their staffs) relate to each other and to the groups.
d7712c0b545a: The Big Book's Appendix VII says it in two lines: "A.A.’s Twelve Steps are principles for personal recovery" and "The Twelve Traditions ensure the unity of the Fellowship" (p. 574). The Concepts are there to keep the service structure "responsive and responsible to those they serve" (p. 574).
f6bdbdebedc6: They are connected. Bill builds the Concepts on the Traditions, Tradition Two above all, and the Twelfth Concept binds the Conference to "observe the spirit of the A.A. Tradition" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).

Traditions as first printed in 1946" (p. 561). They were written while both co-founders were alive.
087796d84215: <0>The Concepts</0> were "Written by co-founder Bill W. in 1962" (p. 574), twelve years after Dr. Bob died, and adopted by the General Service Conference that April. Their one-sentence short form was approved in 1971 and added to the Big Book in the fourth edition, 2001 (p. xii).
d5fc3efd8def: The Long Form of the Traditions talks to groups and members: who may belong (any alcoholic who wants to recover), what makes a group (two or three alcoholics with no other affiliation), group autonomy, the one primary purpose, money, property, outside issues, anonymity (pp. 563–566).
c1d44b47f10c: The Concepts talk to the service bodies. Concept I is about where final authority over "world services" sits; the rest cover the Conference, the trustees, their committees, the two service corporations, executives and paid staff. Bill's introduction says the Concepts set out "the ‘why’ of our service structure" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction).
2e841e61581f: They are also written differently. Bill says that "Since each Concept is really a group of related principles" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction), they could not be made as short as the Steps and Traditions. Each Concept comes with a long essay; the Traditions' Long Form is a paragraph each.
109f2eb1f6eb: Bill doesn't present the Concepts as a second set of Traditions. He presents them as the Traditions applied to A.A.'s service center:
672012c81968: <0>Tradition Two.</0> The Long Form says: "For our group purpose there is but one ultimate authority—a loving God as He may express Himself in our group conscience" (p. 563). Concept I quotes Tradition Two and says its principles are "crystal clear: the A.A. groups are to be the final authority; their leaders are to be entrusted with delegated responsibilities only" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept I). Concepts II, III, IV, V and X all lean on its "trusted servants" line. Tradition Two is the one Bill names throughout. The links below are ours: the essays don't cite these Long Form passages, except that Concept XII grounds its first Warranty in declining outside money and its fifth in the Tradition against public controversy.
743765d72295: <0>Long Form Nine.</0> "The trustees of the General Service Board are, in effect, our A.A. General Service Committee" (p. 565); in 1946 the board was still the Alcoholic Foundation, renamed in 1954. Concepts VI to VIII spell out what those trustees do and don't do.
745645164fa3: <0>Long Form Six and Seven.</0> Property "separately incorporated and managed, thus dividing the material from the spiritual" (p. 564), and treasuries that pile up money "beyond prudent reserves" (p. 564). Concept VIII keeps the service corporations separate; Concept XII's first two Warranties are about wealth and a prudent reserve.
9d6fa7097e26: <0>Long Form Eight.</0> Special workers "may be well recompensed" (p. 564). Concept XI says how paid A.A. staff should be treated and paid.
736ce381de55: <0>Long Form Ten.</0> "The Alcoholics Anonymous groups oppose no one" (p. 565). Concept XII's Fifth Warranty: no public controversy, no punishment.
130e6c1318b4: The Traditions govern A.A. groups and A.A. as a whole. The Concepts were written for the world service structure. Bill does say their principles "can of course be used to good effect throughout our entire structure" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction), and P-8 (1986) says the Warranties express principles that "apply to all other A.A. entities as well" (P-8). But nothing in the Concepts gives anyone authority over a group. Concept XII forbids the Conference "any acts of government" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII), and the Long Form says a group "should be responsible to no other authority than its own conscience" in its own affairs (p. 563).
ff441eeda63a: The Concepts say most of the service structure can be changed easily. Bill notes "that the Conference Charter itself can be easily amended" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction), with an exception or two.
fafa77fe206a: The exceptions are the Traditions and Article 12. The 1955 St. Louis resolution says neither the Traditions nor the Warranties of Article 12 may be changed without asking the registered groups of the world, giving them at least six months, and receiving in writing "the consent of at least three-quarters of all those registered groups who respond to such proposal" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix L). Concept XII is Article 12, which is why Bill writes "We have ranked them therefore with A.A.’s Twelve Traditions" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept XII).
97149be2efe9: One dating detail: the 1955 Charter as first printed asked only for "the written consent of two-thirds of all the A.A. groups" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955) to change the Tradition. The 1957 Conference amended it to three-quarters, matching the St. Louis resolution, and added the Twelve Steps (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, footnote 4). Concepts I to XI have no such protection.

5aaf40c55f4f: What are the Twelve Concepts, and why were they written?
b91cf61d2492: The Twelve Concepts for World Service are twelve statements, each with a long essay, written by Bill W. in 1962 about how A.A.'s world services are run: the groups, the General Service Conference, the trustees of the General Service Board, and the service corporations and their staffs. The 12th General Service Conference adopted them on April 26, 1962.
263ed55c90d0: They are not about personal recovery or about how a group runs itself. The Big Book's Appendix VII puts it in one line each: the Steps are for personal recovery, the Traditions for unity, and the Concepts help keep the service structure "responsive and responsible to those they serve" (p. 574).
093e26f41668: Bill says he wrote them to record the "why" of the service structure so its lessons would not be lost once the founders were gone. Dr. Bob had died in 1950; Bill was preparing to step back.
372195bd5047: They are later than the Traditions (1946) and Dr. Bob's death. Where the 1946–47 texts already state a principle, the Concepts build on it, and these pages show the earlier text first.
4626d7d21253: The Concepts' own title page says they were written "by Bill W." and adopted "by the 12th Annual General Service Conference of Alcoholics Anonymous on April 26, 1962" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, title page).
2e8675e226f5: A 1985 preface from the General Service Office says they "were written by Bill W. in 1962" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Preface, 1985). Details went out of date, so the 1985 Conference asked that they be printed "in the original 1962 version, with required factual changes provided as numbered footnotes at the end of each chapter" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Preface, 1985). That is how our copy reads: Bill's 1962 text, with footnotes added as late as the 2024–2026 edition.
ecd69d451ed5: A one-sentence "short form" of each Concept came later. It was approved by the 1971 Conference and put in the Service Manual in 1974 (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Preface, 1985). The Big Book has printed that short form since the fourth edition (p. xii), as Appendix VII on pages 574–575, which says the Concepts were "Written by co-founder Bill W. in 1962" (p. 574).
c809c487af34: <0>To keep the experience.</0> His introduction says: "These Concepts therefore aim to record the ‘why’ of our service structure" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction). He expected later workers to change things, and warned that "change does not necessarily spell progress" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction). If a change went wrong, the Concepts would be a way back to what had worked.
812879f05e27: <0>Not to freeze it.</0> In the same introduction he rejects the idea that the Concepts should harden into gospel: "Nothing could stray further from the intent of these Concepts" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction). A good enough case, convincing to both the trustees and the Conference, is all a change needs.
44b247e6ca05: <0>Because of power.</0> He built them on "checks and balances" because alcoholics in charge tend to enlarge their own authority, and resist anyone else's. Of those traits he writes: "I’m the more sure of this because I possess these traits myself" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Introduction).
6ad195bd4257: <0>Because the founders would not last.</0> Concept I tells the story. And in Chapter 7, helping others may mean "innumerable trips to police courts, sanitariums, hospitals, jails and asylums" (p. 97). In both, people go to court on a drinker's behalf. The third is in Chapter 6, on amends: a man whose first wife "went to court and got an order for his arrest" (p. 79) over unpaid alimony wrote to her instead of walking up to the judge, and the matter was settled (p. 79). None of the three involves reporting on anyone's attendance.

3c32f04813c2: His main points: the alcoholic's body reacts abnormally to alcohol (his "allergy" theory), the result is a craving the normal drinker never has, the only relief he knows is not drinking at all, and real recovery takes "an entire psychic change" (p. xxix).
419d7a577e3b: The section has three voices: 1. <0>A.A. members</0> open it, introducing "the medical estimate of the plan of recovery described in this book" from a doctor "chief physician at a nationally prominent hospital specializing in alcoholic and drug addiction" (p. xxv). Silkworth, M.D. 3. <2>A.A. members</2> then comment on his views (pp. xxvi–xxvii), and <3>his longer statement</3> follows (pp. xxvii–xxxii), signed again at the end (p. xxxii).
777e5a51d144: Who he was, from the book itself: the Foreword to the Second Edition (1955) calls him "a New York specialist in alcoholism" who had greatly helped Bill W. and from whom Bill "had learned the grave nature of alcoholism" (p. xvi). Comes of Age</0> (1957) adds that he was "then Physician-in-Chief of the Charles B. Towns Hospital in New York," and that he was with Bill in that hospital in December 1934 (<1>Comes of Age</1>, p. 13).
312103be8f89: The letter's patient of "late 1934" (p. xxv) and the "leading contributors to this book" who came under his care (p. xxvii) are not named in the section. <0>Comes of Age</0> identifies Silkworth as the doctor who treated Bill (<1>Comes of Age</1>, p. 13).
0f7f17cf48ee: <0>In his letter</0> (pp. xxv–xxvi): a hopeless patient picked up ideas about recovery and began passing them on to other alcoholics, telling them to do the same, and "This man and over one hundred others appear to have recovered" (p. xxv). 8d9a573e55a5: <0>In his longer statement</0> (pp. xxvii–xxxii): - <1>The body.</1> He suggests that alcohol acts on these drinkers as "a manifestation of an allergy" and that "the phenomenon of craving is limited to this class and never occurs in the average temperate drinker" (p. xxviii). After each spree comes remorse and a firm resolution, and "This is repeated over and over" (p. xxix). - <3>The way out.</3> "The only relief we have to suggest is entire abstinence" (p. xxx). But not drinking takes more than knowledge or willpower: "unless this person can experience an entire psychic change there is very little hope of his recovery" (p. xxix). - <4>What medicine can't do.</4> Doctors, he admits, "have made little impression upon the problem as a whole" (p. xxix). "One feels that something more than human power is needed to produce the essential psychic change" (p. xxix). - <5>Why he backs A.A.</5> He praises the members' unselfishness and "the entire absence of profit motive" (p. xxvii) and says he has found nothing that has done more for these men "than the altruistic movement now growing up among them" (p. xxviii). He closes with two case histories (pp. xxxi–xxxii) and a line every reader of the Big Book knows: the alcoholic who reads it, "though perhaps he came to scoff, he may remain to pray" (p. xxxii).
